long-run-self-adjustment-s1.title: Country G after a fall in spending, with no policy response

table.caption: Country G, four years after a fall in aggregate demand, with no policy response; full-employment real GDP is 1,000 billion dollars and the natural rate of unemployment is 5% (invented data for practice)

items.q: Based on the table, what brings Country G's real GDP back to 1,000 billion dollars?
options: Falling nominal wages lower costs, so SRAS shifts right
Rising spending shifts AD back to the right
A rise in the price level makes production more profitable
LRAS shifts right as the economy grows

why.correct: High unemployment pushes nominal wages down (100 to 95). Lower costs shift SRAS right, so output rises back to 1,000 while the price level falls.
options: Right: with unemployment above the natural rate, wages fall, costs fall and SRAS shifts right until output reaches full employment.
Nothing in the table shows spending recovering. The wage index falls, which works through SRAS.
The price level falls in the table, from 100 to 96.
Full-employment output stays at 1,000 throughout, so LRAS did not move.

items.q: Using the table, calculate the percent change in Country G's nominal wage index from Year 1 to Year 4.

mistakes.why: Wages fell, so the percent change is negative: $-5\%$.
95 is the index in Year 4. The percent change compares it with Year 1: $\frac{95 - 100}{100} \times 100$.

items.q: Based on the table, why did Country G's nominal wages fall from Year 1 to Year 4?
options: The price level was rising, so workers needed lower wages
Unemployment was above the natural rate
Real GDP was above full-employment output
Firms were short of workers and cut wages to hire more

why.correct: In a recessionary gap, unemployment is above the natural rate. Over time, contracts are renegotiated at lower nominal wages.
options: The price level fell. Wages fell because of high unemployment.
Right: a surplus of workers puts downward pressure on nominal wages.
Real GDP was below 1,000 until Year 4, a recessionary gap.
Shortages of workers push wages up. There were too many job seekers here.

items.q: Based on the table, in which year is Country G back in long-run equilibrium?
options: Year 1
Year 2
Year 4
Year 3

why.correct: Long-run equilibrium returns when output equals full-employment output and unemployment equals the natural rate: Year 4.
options: Year 1 has the largest gap: 900 against 1,000.
Output (940) is still below full employment.
Right: real GDP equals full-employment output (1,000) and unemployment equals the natural rate (5%).
Output (970) is still below 1,000 and unemployment (6%) above the natural rate.

items.q: If no policy is used, what happens to nominal wages in Country H over time, and why?
options: They fall, because output is above full employment
They stay the same, because wages are sticky
They rise, because AD keeps shifting right
They rise, as labor is scarce

why.correct: Country H is in an inflationary gap: unemployment is below the natural rate, so nominal wages rise over time.
options: Output above full employment means scarce labor, which pushes wages up, not down.
Wages are sticky only in the short run; given time, contracts are renegotiated.
The graph shows no further shift in AD. Wages rise because labor is scarce.
Right: output is above full employment, labor is scarce, and wages are bid up as contracts are renewed.

items.q: In Country H, which curve shifts as the economy adjusts on its own, and in which direction?
options: SRAS shifts left
SRAS shifts right
AD shifts left
LRAS shifts right

why.correct: Rising nominal wages and input prices shift SRAS left: the self-adjustment always runs through SRAS.
options: Right: higher nominal wages raise costs, so SRAS shifts left until it meets AD on LRAS.
Rising wages raise costs, which shift SRAS left, not right.
The adjustment works through wages and costs, which are SRAS, not through spending.
LRAS moves with resources and technology, which have not changed.

items.q: Once Country H has fully adjusted, how do its price level and real GDP compare with today?
options: The price level is lower and real GDP is lower
The price level is higher and real GDP is lower
The price level is higher and real GDP is higher
Both are the same as today, since the gap closes itself

why.correct: From an inflationary gap, SRAS shifts left: the price level rises further and real GDP falls back to YF.
options: A leftward SRAS shift raises the price level.
Right: SRAS shifts left along AD until output equals full-employment output.
Real GDP falls back to full-employment output from above it.
Closing the gap moves the economy: output falls to YF and the price level rises.

items.q: This economy is in a recessionary gap and no policy is used. Show the long-run adjustment: shift the right curve and mark the new equilibrium.

why.correct: Unemployment above the natural rate lowers nominal wages and input prices, so SRAS shifts right: the price level falls and real GDP rises to full employment.

key.because: a fall in nominal wages and input prices

slips.AD: Left alone, the economy does not change its spending. It adjusts through nominal wages and input prices, which shift SRAS.

items.q: This economy is in an inflationary gap and no policy is used. Show the long-run adjustment: shift the right curve and mark the new equilibrium.

why.correct: Unemployment below the natural rate raises nominal wages and input prices, so SRAS shifts left: the price level rises and real GDP falls to full employment.

key.because: a rise in nominal wages and input prices

slips.AD: Left alone, the economy does not change its spending. It adjusts through nominal wages and input prices, which shift SRAS.

items.q: The economy starts in long-run equilibrium. Exports boom and stay high. Show both the short-run shift and the long-run adjustment, and mark the final equilibrium.

why.correct: AD shifts right (short run), then rising wages shift SRAS left (long run). Output returns to full employment at a higher price level.

key.because: an export boom, then rising wages

items.q: Put the links of self-adjustment from a recessionary gap in order.
options: Real GDP is below full-employment output
Unemployment is above the natural rate
Nominal wages and input prices fall as contracts are renewed
SRAS shifts right
Real GDP rises to full-employment output and the price level falls

why.correct: The gap causes high unemployment, which lowers wages and costs, which shifts SRAS right until output reaches YF.

items.q: Make it specific: explain how an economy in an inflationary gap returns to full employment with no policy.

why.correct: Labor is scarce, so nominal wages rise; SRAS shifts left until output is back at full employment, at a higher price level.

specific.frame: Unemployment is ___ the natural rate, so nominal wages ___. ___ shifts to the ___ until real GDP equals full-employment output, and the price level ___.
specific.model: Unemployment is below the natural rate, so nominal wages rise because firms compete for scarce workers. Higher costs shift SRAS to the left until real GDP equals full-employment output, and the price level rises.

unemployment.label: Unemployment
options: below
above

why.1: Output above full employment means more jobs, so unemployment is below the natural rate.

change.label: Nominal wages
options: rise
fall

curve.label: The curve
options: SRAS
AD

why.1: Self-adjustment works through wages and costs, which shift SRAS; spending does not change.

direction.label: Which way
options: left
right

why.1: Higher costs mean less output supplied at each price level.

price.label: Price level
options: rises
falls

why.1: SRAS moving left along AD raises the price level.

items.q: A student writes: "In a recessionary gap, the economy returns to full employment because aggregate demand recovers." What is wrong with this as an explanation of long-run self-adjustment?
options: Self-adjustment works through rising nominal wages shifting SRAS left
Nothing is wrong: AD shifts right as people regain confidence
It names AD; the mechanism is falling wages shifting SRAS right
Self-adjustment works through LRAS shifting left to meet AD

why.correct: The mechanism readers look for: unemployment above the natural rate lowers nominal wages and input prices, so SRAS shifts right.
options: Rising wages describe an inflationary gap. In a recessionary gap wages fall.
If spending recovers that is a new demand shock, not self-adjustment, which runs through wages and SRAS.
Right: with no policy, spending is unchanged; lower wages and input prices shift SRAS.
LRAS depends on resources and technology, which did not change.

items.q: In the long run, what is the effect of a lasting rise in aggregate demand, starting from full employment?
options: A higher price level and higher real GDP
The same price level with higher real GDP
A lower price level with real GDP back at full employment
A higher price level with real GDP back at full-employment output

why.correct: In the long run, AD changes affect the price level but not real GDP: output returns to LRAS.
options: That is the short run. In the long run wages rise and output returns to YF.
In the long run output is set by LRAS; more spending only raises prices.
The long-run adjustment from an inflationary gap raises the price level further.
Right: wages catch up and SRAS shifts left, so only the price level stays higher.

items.q: A drought shifts SRAS left and the economy falls into a recessionary gap. If the drought ends and no policy is used, how does the economy return to full employment?
options: Lower wages and input prices shift SRAS back right
Rising prices raise profits, so firms hire more until output is back
AD shifts left to meet LRAS
LRAS shifts left to meet the new equilibrium

why.correct: With output below full employment, wages and input prices fall and SRAS shifts right until output is back at YF.
options: Right: the same SRAS mechanism closes a gap however it began.
In a recessionary gap the price level falls as SRAS shifts right.
A leftward AD shift would lower output further.
LRAS moves only with resources and technology. A temporary drought does not lower capacity for good.

items.q: Why can self-adjustment out of a recessionary gap take a long time?
options: LRAS has to shift right first
Nominal wages are slow to fall
AD has to shift left before SRAS can move
The price level has to rise before wages can fall

why.correct: Wage contracts last months or years and employers avoid cutting pay, so nominal wages adjust slowly downward.
options: LRAS does not need to move; SRAS shifts to meet it.
Right: wages are especially sticky downward, so SRAS can take years to shift right.
AD does not need to move at all for self-adjustment.
The price level falls during self-adjustment from a recessionary gap.

items.q: An economy is in a recessionary gap and no policy is used. Which of the following is part of how it returns to full employment? Select all that apply.
options: Nominal wages and input prices fall, shifting SRAS right
Spending recovers and AD shifts right
LRAS shifts left to meet the current output
The price level rises, making production more profitable

why.correct: Self-adjustment from a recessionary gap: unemployment above the natural rate lowers nominal wages and input prices, and SRAS shifts right.
options: Right: this is the self-adjustment mechanism.
With no policy, spending is unchanged; the adjustment runs through SRAS.
LRAS depends on resources and technology, which did not change.
As SRAS shifts right, the price level falls.
